title: The rich fool (Luke 12:16–21)
hook: a man plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night

segments.voice: Yesterday, the talents, and the word talent: a weight of silver, and one servant who buried his in the ground. Your line was fear buries things. Did you dig one gift up? Day thirty.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. And Jesus won't referee. Instead, he tells a story. A rich man's land has a bumper year. More grain than he's ever seen. More than his barns can hold. So he lies awake, and he talks it over with himself. What shall I do? I know. I'll tear down my barns and build bigger ones. I'll store everything. And then I'll say to my soul: you're set for years. Relax. Eat, drink, enjoy. It's a good plan. Any financial advisor would sign off on it. And that same night, God speaks to him, for the only time in the story, and calls him a fool. Today, the rich fool.
screen: `SPLIT THE INHERITANCE.` → `A BUMPER YEAR.` → `BIGGER BARNS.` → `THAT SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Listen to how the man talks. In a few sentences he says I, my and mine again and again: my crops, my barns, my fruits, my goods, my soul. There's nobody else in his plan. No family, no workers, no neighbor. He even talks to his own soul, like it's the only person in the room. The old King James Bible gives his words: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." And then the answer: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?" Notice what he isn't. He isn't a thief. He didn't cheat anyone; the land just produced. Saving for the future isn't the problem either; the Bible praises the ant for storing food. The fool's mistake is quieter. He thinks the barn is his life. Jesus says it plainly just before the story: a man's life doesn't consist in the abundance of the things he owns. The word fool here doesn't mean stupid. He's clearly clever. In the Bible a fool is someone who lives as if God weren't there. And look at the question God asks: then whose shall those things be? He's about to leave it all to someone else, which is exactly what the brother in the crowd was fighting over. Luke ends the story with one more line: so is anyone who stores up treasure for himself and isn't rich toward God. Christians have heard rich toward God as generosity, prayer, and a life turned outward. Luke's answer, a few verses on, is simple: give.
screen: `I, MY, MINE.` · `NOT A THIEF. NOT A CHEAT.` · `HE THINKS THE BARN IS HIS LIFE.` · `WHOSE SHALL THOSE THINGS BE?` · then, large: `RICH TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you're only storing. Settle, and breathe. Walk through your home in your mind. The closet. The drawer you don't open. The shelf in the garage. Find one thing you're keeping just to keep it. A coat you never wear. A book you've finished. Picture who could use it. If you pray, you can ask where it should go. If you don't, just picture it leaving your barn and landing somewhere it's needed. The bell holds the time.
The rich fool. Not a thief, just a man who built bigger barns for himself and forgot that his life was more than what he owned.
Your line: you can't take the barn. Today, give away the one thing you found. A coat, a book, a tool. Out of the barn and into somebody's hands. Day thirty.

howItsDone: Many Christians read this parable as a warning against greed and a call to generosity, and it's often preached alongside giving to the poor, tithing, or simplifying how they live.

tear down my barns, build bigger ones, and take it easy for years.

fork.reveal: he builds bigger barns and tells his soul to eat, drink and be merry. that night God calls him a fool: "then whose shall those things be?"

original.note: Greek: fool. literally "without mind," someone who doesn't think things through.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story that says being rich is wrong.
what it means: a man who thinks his barn is his life, and plans a future with nobody else in it.

what a scholar hears: aphrōn, fool, the word the Psalms use for someone who lives as if there is no God. and the question it ends on, whose shall those things be, answers the brother fighting over an inheritance.

notes: 'The Bible praises the ant for storing food' refers to Proverbs 6:6–8; confirm the aside is welcome.

'In the Bible a fool is someone who lives as if God weren't there' leans on Psalm 14:1 / 53:1 ('The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God'). The Greek Septuagint of Psalm 14:1 uses ἄφρων; please confirm the trapdoor link.
'Luke's answer, a few verses on, is simple: give' refers to Luke 12:33 (sell what you have and give alms); paraphrased. Confirm.
Count of 'I / my' is left unnumbered ('again and again') on purpose; the KJV has many first-person pronouns in 12:17–19.
Hook: 'God speaks to him, for the only time in the story' — God speaks only once in the parable; confirm wording.
